articles.title: Are the Houthis attacking Mecca and Medina? Saudi claims ignite battle over Islam's holiest cities - Ynetnews
articles.summary: Are the Houthis attacking Mecca and Medina? Saudi claims ignite battle over Islam's holiest cities  YnetnewsIran war updates: Houthis target Riyadh as coalition intercepts missiles  Al JazeeraSaudi-led coalition says it downs drone over oil-rich Eastern Region  ReutersSaudi Arabia says at least 2 suspected Houthi drones shot down over kingdom  The Times of IsraelSaudi-led coalition launches operation to ‘neutralize’ Houthi military resources in Yemen ...
articles.full_text:
Houthi forces have been attacking Saudi Arabia relentlessly in recent months, launching missiles and drones toward targets including the capital Riyadh and the areas of Al-Kharj, Jeddah, Yanbu, Khamis Mushait and Najran. But when it comes to alleged attacks on Mecca and Medina, Islam's two holiest cities, the facts are far less clear. In recent weeks, Saudi authorities have repeatedly reported air raid alerts in both cities, while the Houthis have vehemently denied targeting either of them. For Muslims, Sunni and Shiite alike, the religious significance of the two cities is profound, as are the implications of attacking them.
Within the broader war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, another battle is now unfolding over which side is violating the sanctity of Islam's holiest sites and behaving like an "enemy of Islam."
On Friday morning, the Saudi-led coalition reported intercepting a drone that it said had been launched by the Houthis toward Mecca. Hours later, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree dismissed the allegation as fabricated. "Our operations target their oil facilities and military bases, and no one in the world believes these lies and fabrications," he said. Later that day, the coalition announced that it had intercepted another drone in the Medina area, prompting another Houthi denial.
Mecca is Islam's holiest city, regarded as the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad and home to the Grand Mosque, or Masjid al-Haram, the most sacred mosque in Islam. Within it stands the Kaaba, the ancient structure toward which Muslims around the world face during their daily prayers and the focal point of the annual Hajj pilgrimage. Medina, Islam's second-holiest city, is where Muhammad migrated from Mecca in an event known as the Hijra. It is also home to the Prophet's Mosque, where he is buried.
The Houthis regularly emphasize their connection to Islam and the Prophet Muhammad. In August, they held celebrations marking the Prophet's birthday in areas under their control. From the group's perspective, Saudi accusations that it is attacking Mecca and Medina amount to allegations that it is threatening Islam's most sacred places. The Houthis insist that Riyadh is exploiting the cities' religious significance for political purposes, while accusing the Saudi authorities themselves of violating their sanctity.
Claims and denials
The war of competing narratives has continued for weeks. The current round of escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began in July, while Saudi allegations of launches toward Mecca first emerged on September 15, when authorities reported alerts in several areas of the kingdom, including the holy city. The Houthi-affiliated Saba news agency quoted a military source categorically rejecting the accusation. "We strongly deny the existence of any threat from Yemen against the holy city of Mecca or any other sacred sites," the source said. "Promoting these reports is intended to tarnish our image and win sympathy from the Islamic world, a familiar tactic of the Saudi enemy."
Mohammed al-Farah, a member of the Houthi political bureau, also rejected the accusations. "The talk of an attack on Mecca from Yemen is a lie," he said. "Saudi Arabia is facing a real crisis. It is begging the international community and trying to mobilize Muslims using a false pretext to divert attention from its failure. The solution is clear: Stop the aggression, lift the blockade, leave Yemen alone and compensate Yemenis for the years of war and destruction."
The Saudi-led coalition subsequently issued a statement indicating that the alert in Mecca had been triggered by a Houthi drone launched toward the city and intercepted outside its boundaries. "This hostile attempt marks the second time Mecca has been attacked, following an initial attempt to launch a ballistic missile on July 27, 2017," the coalition said. It described the alleged attack as "a black stain on the history of the Houthis" and an attempt to provoke the religious feelings of millions of Muslims, stressing that "the security of the Two Holy Mosques is a red line."
On September 17, Houthi leader Abdul-Malik Badr al-Din al-Houthi rejected the Saudi accusation, saying the alleged attack was an invention that itself violated the sanctity of Mecca, a city sacred to all Muslims, particularly Yemenis. The following day, Houthi supporters demonstrated in areas under the group's control against Saudi Arabia and what they called "the lie about attacking Mecca." The denials continued into October. In a statement on October 16, Saree said: "The lies spread by the Saudi regime about targeting holy Mecca are fooling no one. They are the ones desecrating the holy city through immorality and debauchery. Yemen poses no threat to the holy sites. Our operations are directed against the regime's oil facilities and military bases, which are far from the holy places."
The Houthi political bureau also denied targeting Mecca, describing the accusation as "the biggest lie of our time." It said Mecca and all Islamic holy sites hold a sacred place in the hearts of Muslim peoples, particularly Yemenis, while accusing the Saudi authorities of exploiting the cities' religious significance for warfare. The statement also alleged that Saudi Arabia was desecrating Mecca by "hosting Zionist Jews," as the Houthis put it, and organizing parties characterized by debauchery and moral corruption. "The Saudi regime remembers the sanctity of Mecca only when it needs to exploit the holy sites to serve its positions," it said. Yemeni cartoonist and Houthi supporter Kamal Sharaf joined the campaign with a cartoon and video intended to demonstrate that the Houthis were attacking Aramco, the Saudi oil company, rather than the Kaaba.
‘An unforgivable act’: Turkey and Pakistan back Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia's partners in the "Mecca Defense Alliance," Turkey and Pakistan, backed Riyadh in the dispute. Pakistan's Foreign Ministry issued an official statement condemning the alleged Houthi attack on Mecca, while Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed outrage in a post on X on October 16. "The people of Pakistan feel deep sorrow and concern over this act," he wrote. "Words cannot describe the depth of the pain and grief we feel over this unforgivable act. We salute the vigilance, courage and professionalism of the Saudi forces for their swift action."
"Pakistan stands with Saudi Arabia in defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity, and in ensuring the security and sanctity of the Two Holy Mosques, a duty that every Pakistani carries deep in their heart," Sharif added. Turkey also issued official condemnations following the reports of an attempted attack on Mecca.
The allegations continued over the following weeks. On October 21, the Houthi military spokesman responded to a Saudi-led coalition announcement that drones had been intercepted, including in the Medina area. "The armed forces carried out no military operations deep inside Saudi Arabia today," Saree said. "The Saudi enemy's claim that drones were intercepted over Medina is a lie and a smear against our honorable and courageous people and armed forces."
On October 24, Saudi Civil Defense reported debris falling in several locations following the interception of two ballistic missiles allegedly launched by the Houthis toward the Mecca and Medina regions. According to the Saudi account, fragments fell in Wadi al-Marmas in Mecca, the Al-Nuzha neighborhood in the Jeddah area, Wadi Jalil in the Taif area and the Rabigh district. The Houthis again denied targeting the holy cities, maintaining that their military operations were directed against oil facilities and military bases. In recent weeks, Houthi officials have also repeatedly warned that Saudi airspace is "unsafe," while explicitly excluding the skies over Mecca and Medina from those threats.
On Friday, Houthi government spokesman Omar al-Buhaiti brought Israel into the dispute, alleging that Saudi Arabia and its "Zionist partner" were plotting to attack Islamic holy sites and blame Yemen. "The Saudi enemy's repeated claim that Yemen has attempted to target holy sites reveals malicious intentions already harbored by the Saudi enemy and its Zionist partner," he said. "We hold the Saudi regime fully responsible for any harm, attack or plot targeting the holy sites in Mecca and Medina." He warned that any attack on the Two Holy Mosques by what he called the Saudi enemy would have "devastating consequences" for Riyadh. The accusations against Israel were made without supporting evidence.
Where does the truth lie? ‘The Saudis have an interest’
For now, Saudi Arabia continues to accuse the Houthis, and the Houthis continue to issue categorical denials. But conclusive evidence that Mecca and Medina themselves have been targeted remains lacking. That raises a fundamental question: Are the Houthis really aiming at the two cities, and would they have any reason to attack places that hold such profound religious significance for them as well?
Dr. Yoel Guzansky, a former Israeli National Security Council official and senior researcher who heads the Gulf program at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told ynet that the issue is exceptionally sensitive. He questioned whether the Houthis had actually fired toward the two cities. "It is completely contrary to the Houthis' interests, because doing so could unite the entire Islamic world in opposition to them," he said.
"The Saudis have an interest in showing that the Houthis are attacking Islam's holy sites, Mecca and Medina," Guzansky explained. "That could help them mobilize legitimacy and international support, especially from Pakistan, Turkey and other countries whose assistance Saudi Arabia wants. It could be presented as, 'Here we are, coming to defend Islam's holy sites because Saudi Arabia is in trouble.'"

articles.title: Trump threatens to strike 'one or two targets' still left in Iran
articles.summary: The U.S. had destroyed much of Iran’s military but still needed to "take care of" one or two targets, President Donald Trump said Saturday, as Tehran warned of retaliation if attac...
articles.full_text:
The U.S. had destroyed much of Iran’s military but still needed to "take care of" one or two targets, President Donald Trump said Saturday, as Tehran warned of retaliation if attacked.
Trump said negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the United States and Israel in February, were "going fine, but you know they're not very reliable."
He added that the U.S. was not in a hurry to take offensive action because it had already decimated Iran's military and nuclear program.
"We've knocked out their nuclear program. We still have to take care of one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes," Trump told reporters at his Florida residence.
"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
The Iranian government denied any nuclear work was carried out there.
Earlier Saturday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump had not made a decision about fresh strikes on Iran and that the United States would be open to a diplomatic solution.
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei Saturday warned the United States and Israel against launching a new offensive, following threats they could resume strikes after crucial elections in both countries.
Trump had previously warned an attack could come after the U.S. midterms this week, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke of a "historic, one-time opportunity" to topple the Iranian government.
The elections in both countries could determine the direction of the conflict. Israel voted in a general election Tuesday but had yet to form a new government.
"Any level or type of threat requires an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response," Khamenei told top military commanders in a statement.
He also ordered commanders to update Iran's target list to include "all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy."
This was the first reported meeting between Khamenei and top military commanders.
The supreme leader had not been seen publicly since before he took the helm in March, after the killing of his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in U.S.-Israeli strikes.
Rubio warned that "we can achieve military objectives if we seek to do so," adding that Trump had not made a decision on any fresh strikes.
Since the recent outbreak of the war, Tehran had restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries around one-fifth of global oil consumption.
Iran had previously warned it would also consider severing undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz.
A ship traversing the strait struck a mine and caught fire, Iranian state television reported Saturday.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Friday three oil tankers were halted after encountering unspecified "incidents" or hitting mines.
The blockade had caused a spike in global energy prices, making the war unpopular among the U.S. public ahead of the upcoming polls.
Gains for the opposition Democrats could somewhat restrict Trump's ability to enact policy.
Voting in Israel had left Netanyahu's political camp with the most seats in parliament but short of a majority, leaving the makeup of the next administration unclear.
Fresh diplomatic efforts were underway to avert any resumption of fighting.
Qatari mediators landed in Tehran Friday, and U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance sent a letter to Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.
"'I had not yet responded. Their tone had completely changed," Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said in a video broadcast on Iranian television, describing it as "a good sign" without elaborating.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there were no plans for meetings with U.S. officials.
"Iran's conditions were clear, and consultations regarding them were ongoing among mediators," he said in an interview with Al Jazeera.
Rezaei insisted Iran would continue to blockade the Strait of Hormuz until its conditions, including releasing frozen assets, were met.
Qatar and Pakistan had been mediating between the warring parties, but the talks had yet to produce a lasting agreement.
Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia said any resumption of hostilities would only expand the scope of the war.
"The flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area," he said on social media.
Araghchi posted on X that there would no longer be any "red lines."

articles.title: Child among 8 killed in fresh Israeli violation of Gaza truce
articles.summary: Israeli strikes killed eight Palestinians, including a child and five police officers, in the Gaza Strip Sunday, according to local hospitals, emergency services and the territory’...
articles.full_text:
Israeli strikes killed eight Palestinians, including a child and five police officers, in the Gaza Strip Sunday, according to local hospitals, emergency services and the territory’s Interior Ministry.
Five people were killed in an airstrike in al-Mawasi, west of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, a medical source at Nasser Hospital told Türkiye's Anadolu Agency (AA). The Interior Ministry identified the five as police officers.
"Occupation aircraft targeted several on-duty police officers," the ministry said.
Local sources told AA that the strike hit near schools, causing panic among children.
In Gaza City, a separate strike on al-Thawra Street killed three Palestinians, including a child, and wounded six others, a medical source at al-Shifa Hospital said. Local sources said an Israeli drone targeted a gathering of civilians.
Gaza’s civil defense service confirmed the death tolls in both locations. Local hospitals said they had received the bodies and several wounded people.
The Israeli military claimed it struck several Hamas members in Khan Younis without providing further details. In comments to Agence France-Presse (AFP), it acknowledged strikes in northern and southern Gaza, adding that it was examining the results.
Israel has stepped up strikes in recent weeks, alleging Hamas was rearming and launching attacks in violation of a year-old cease-fire.
Hamas, on the other hand, denies trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal and accuses Israel of undermining the agreement.
Since the cease-fire took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, Israeli attacks have killed 1,580 Palestinians and wounded 5,711 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. Israel says four soldiers have died during that period.
The U.S.-brokered agreement calls for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but negotiations have made little progress toward an agreement on Hamas’ disarmament or the withdrawal of Israeli troops.
Israeli forces control about two-thirds of the territory and have ordered residents to leave those areas. With around 90% of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure destroyed, nearly all of Gaza’s more than 2 million residents are crowded into the remaining third. Many live in makeshift tents or damaged buildings amid the ruins of the war.
Israel’s genocidal war has killed more than 74,500 Palestinians, mostly women and children, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, whose figures the United Nations considers reliable. The ministry has also reported more than 175,000 wounded.
The war was triggered by the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion that caused 1,200 deaths in southern Israel.

articles.title: Campaigning enters homestretch before key US midterm elections
articles.summary: The battle for control of Congress entered its final campaign weekend as President Donald Trump’s administration pursued a criminal investigation into Alaska’s pivotal U.S. Senate...
articles.full_text:
The battle for control of Congress entered its final campaign weekend as President Donald Trump’s administration pursued a criminal investigation into Alaska’s pivotal U.S. Senate race and said Saturday it would likely take a dispute over thousands of California mail-in ballots to the Supreme Court.
In Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating whether aides to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola helped recruit a retired schoolteacher, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to run because his name is similar to Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan.
The closely contested race is crucial to Democrats' hopes of taking the Senate in Tuesday's election.
It is one of 35 Senate races, along with all 435 House seats, that will decide whether U.S. President Donald Trump's Republicans keep control of Congress for the next two years.
Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority and a narrow edge in the House.
Early voting has set a record. More than 51 million Americans have already cast ballots in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day at the last midterms in 2022.
In California, a federal appeals court this week ruled 2-1 that the Justice Department had failed to justify its emergency bid to force the state to set aside mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters it alleges are likely noncitizens.
"I hesitate to give a final answer, but I think probably the Supreme Court is next on this one," acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told Fox News Saturday, adding that any request for Supreme Court consideration would come before Tuesday's election.
U.S. President Donald Trump has been on a campaign blitz in multiple states over the past month but is spending Saturday at his Mar-a-Lago Club in Palm Beach, Florida. He returns to the campaign trail Sunday in Kansas and Iowa.
The Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a Friday news conference that a recent New York Times article, which reported an effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., drove a "surge" of FBI resources to the case.
Heyman said he assigned several prosecutors to it and that investigative steps proceeded "intensely and swiftly."
Peltola and the campaign committee have denied involvement in any effort to recruit the second Sullivan. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign.
Voters in Alaska have largely dismissed the fight over the ballot.
"I knew which Dan Sullivan was which Dan Sullivan, you know? It is very clear on the ballot," Anchorage resident Mickey Buster, 36, said as he stood outside a polling place Saturday.
But another Anchorage voter, Carol Riggs, 52, said she was disappointed by the entire situation and the possibility it "muddies the water for some voters, potentially."
In Michigan, where Democrat Abdul el-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in another closely watched Senate race, el-Sayed's feud with the rival he beat in the primary, U.S. Representative Haley Stevens, flared again.
El-Sayed's campaign asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as "not to distract from the central issues of the campaign," a person familiar with the matter said.
Stevens has backed el-Sayed but demanded he condemn an outside group's ad blaming Israel for high grocery prices and apologize for past rhetoric about Israel.
"It is certainly unhelpful to the el-Sayed campaign to have continued visible division within the party just before Election Day," said Matt Grossmann, a political scientist at Michigan State University. Polls show el-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support.
The administration, beyond its bid to block the counting of ballots from more than 20,000 California voters it alleges are likely noncitizens, has sued roughly 30 states and the District of Columbia seeking unredacted voter rolls.
The legal maneuvers have alarmed state election officials. Under the Constitution, states have primary authority over how states run elections.
On Friday, a federal judge ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening to prosecute California election officials who defy its directives.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, on Saturday warned the state's top federal judges that the Justice Department may seek warrants to seize ballots before results are certified, though he said he did not know of any pending request.
Newsom said in a letter to the judges that the only reason to seize ballots "would be to interfere" in the count.
Sean Morales-Doyle of the Brennan Center for Justice said the efforts, while unlikely to win in court, aim at "creating uncertainty, sowing fear, distrust, chaos," in hopes of pressuring officials such as Alaska's lieutenant governor "to do something that they are not supposed to do."
Even so, 76% of U.S. voters are confident their ballots will be counted accurately, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted from Sept. 30 to Oct. 5, with confidence about equally high among Republicans and Democrats.

articles.title: India's capital hit by new wave of protests over voters list revision
articles.summary: Thousands rallied in India’s capital Sunday in an opposition-led protest demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief over a voter list overhaul they say unfairly favo...
articles.full_text:
Thousands rallied in India’s capital Sunday in an opposition-led protest demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief over a voter list overhaul they say unfairly favors the ruling party.
The nationwide revision of electoral rolls has sparked political disputes and street protests in the world's largest democracy over the past month.
The Election Commission says the initiative is necessary to ensure accurate voter rolls, but the opposition claims it is being manipulated to favor Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Both the Election Commission and the BJP deny the accusations.
On Sunday, protesters led by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of the Congress party chanted "vote thief, leave your seat" and beat drums while marching from central New Delhi to Ramlila Maidan, a large outdoor venue.
"I have been a voter since I was 18 and now I find myself removed from the list," protester Nandita, 46, said, who gave only one name.
"It's important to be here because of the way things are going. The cost of living is going up. The only option is to take to the streets peacefully," she added.
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online youth-led protest movement, has also thrown its weight behind the campaign against the voter roll revision.
The overhaul of India's voter rolls led to the removal of more than 133 million names, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings.
Critics say the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.
Members of the Hindu-nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighboring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India's voter rolls.
Election authorities say the revision was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries and that eligible voters remain entitled to apply for inclusion on the voter rolls.
Human Rights Watch said the removal of voters was "arbitrary and deeply flawed."
"The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India's most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services," it said in a statement this week.
The CJP has been heavily involved in the pushback to the voter roll revision and police temporarily detained several of its leaders during protests last month.
The CJP has gained millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May.
Earlier protests organized by the CJP in July over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climb down by Modi's administration.

articles.title: Mass riots, looting in Germany mar nationwide Gen-Z protests
articles.summary: Nationwide youth-led protests in Germany were marred by rioting, looting and attacks on police Saturday as largely peaceful daytime demonstrations gave way to serious unrest in Fra...
articles.full_text:
Nationwide youth-led protests in Germany were marred by rioting, looting and attacks on police Saturday as largely peaceful daytime demonstrations gave way to serious unrest in Frankfurt and Cologne that evening.
Rioters smashed shop windows, looted stores, and threw Molotov cocktails at police in central Frankfurt. In Cologne, attackers threw bottles and bicycles at officers near the city's famous cathedral.
Politicians and police blamed the violence on groups of masked, radical left-wing activists.
Unrest followed demonstrations by tens of thousands of young Germans demanding better schools, relief from rising living costs, and greater social justice. Protesters also vented anger at conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Many protests were peaceful.
Participants carried placards with slogans including "Our future is not for sale," "System change, not climate change," "Education, not bombs," and "Eat the rich."
The "Gen Z regelt" (Gen Z Takes Charge) initiative had expected demonstrations in more than 30 German cities, drawing inspiration from weeks of large-scale youth demonstrations in France and elsewhere in Europe. Despite strong interest on social media and widespread media coverage, turnout was more modest than anticipated.
Before the evening's chaos, organizers hailed the protests as a success, reporting more than 100,000 participants nationwide in major cities and smaller centers like Erfurt, Münster, Nuremberg and Karlsruhe.
Nationwide police figures were unavailable, though individual cities released their own turnout tallies.
Frankfurt experienced some of the worst scenes. Rioters smashed shop windows and broke into stores to steal trainers and other goods, dpa journalists observed.
Rioters attacked a specialist firearms shop late Saturday. Police arrested several people and recovered two weapons from the store. Officials did not specify the type of weapons.
Rioters also set trash bins on fire, tore down street signs and smashed shop windows with signs and other objects.
Police reported Molotov cocktails were thrown at officers as violent clashes continued downtown.
At about 10 p.m., officers sealed off a section of the Zeil, one of Germany's busiest shopping streets and urged people to avoid the area.
Authorities deployed special police units (SEK) as unrest continued late into the night. Authorities said more than 1,000 security personnel deployed downtown shortly before midnight. Police reported about 30 people taken into custody.
Earlier, up to 8,000 people joined a largely peaceful demonstration, police said, while organizers estimated turnout at about 9,000.
The protests began in the afternoon on the banks of the Main river near the European Central Bank. The procession moved through central Frankfurt for several kilometers over several hours. Organizers urged participants to remain peaceful.
However, the situation deteriorated hours later when police came under repeated attack with stones, bottles, and firecrackers.
Officers used water cannons and broke up the demonstration in the early evening, but violent groups remained active downtown after many peaceful protesters left.
Hesse state Interior Minister Roman Poseck said several police officers were injured, adding that one officer may have suffered more serious injuries.
Poseck said about 100 suspected left-wing extremists were responsible for the evening violence.
In Cologne, about 200 people, including some rioters, were involved in disturbances around the city's cathedral, next to the main railway station.
Attackers threw bottles and bicycles at police officers during the unrest. One person was injured.
Five people were detained, police said.
In a nearby side street, someone smashed a window with a thrown electric scooter.
After repeated clashes, police dispersed the large crowd outside the cathedral to deescalate the situation. However, smaller groups continued moving downtown, with occasional fireworks set off.
A police spokeswoman said the later incidents appeared linked more to Halloween celebrations than to the earlier youth protests.
Disturbances were also reported in other cities.
In Berlin, police broke up an evening demonstration after officers were attacked with stones and protesters set off fireworks. Police said 27 officers suffered minor injuries and up to 56 demonstrators were temporarily detained.
About 700 people initially gathered at Rosenthaler Platz downtown for a march under the slogan "Gen Z Has Had Enough!" toward Prenzlauer Berg. The crowd grew to as many as 3,500 participants, police said.
Police said the atmosphere was tense from the outset, with many participants dressed in black and wearing masks. Groups on the political left organized the march, and pro-Palestinian activists also took part.
After police ended the demonstration early in coordination with organizers, smaller groups continued moving through nearby streets.
"It's now like a game of cat and mouse," police spokesperson Julia Scholz said. The situation calmed by about 8 p.m.
The evening march was separate from the main "Gen Z regelt" demonstration, where up to 5,000 people gathered peacefully at the Brandenburg Gate earlier in the day.
In Hamburg, a largely peaceful demonstration of about 6,700 people was followed by disturbances near the main railway station.
People dressed in black, some with covered faces, set off fireworks, tore down plastic construction barriers, and set them on fire. Police used water cannons to extinguish the flames and pepper spray to disperse the crowd.
In Bremen, where about 2,800 people demonstrated, isolated incidents included officers being punched and kicked, and at least one trash container set alight.
